title: Printing Variables
summary: Mix text and values in output with Println, string concatenation, Printf verbs, field widths, and Sprintf.
intro: Real programs print values, not just fixed text. Go gives you `fmt.Println` with several arguments, `+` to join strings, and `fmt.Printf` and `fmt.Sprintf` with verbs that control exactly how each value looks.

steps.title: Println and +
steps.body:
You already know that `fmt.Println` joins its arguments with single spaces and ends the line. The arguments can be any mix of text and values, not only strings. Numbers, strings, and bools all work, so this is the quickest way to label a value.

```go
fmt.Println("Score:", 42) // Score: 42
```

To glue strings together with no space added, use `+`. It builds a new string. Go strings never change, so `+` copies the pieces into fresh memory and leaves the originals alone.

```go
name := "Sam"
greeting := "Hi, " + name + "!" // Hi, Sam!
```

The gotcha: `+` only joins a string with another string. It never turns a number into text for you, so this is a compile error, not a runtime surprise:

```go
fmt.Println("Age: " + 30) // does not compile
```

Wrapping the number in `string(...)` does not help either: `string` of an int gives the character with that code, not its digits. When a line mixes text and numbers, pass them as separate `Println` arguments, or use `Printf` from the next step.

example.title: Name card
example.prompt: Print a name and an age with one Println call, then print a greeting built with +.
example.explanation: `Println` gets four arguments and puts a space between each, so the int `age` prints right next to its label. The greeting uses `+` because every piece is a string, and `+` adds no spaces, so the comma and the space live inside the quotes.

practice.title: Weather line
practice.prompt:
Print a city and its temperature, then a welcome line.

1. Keep `city := "Oslo"` and `temp := -3`.
2. Print `City: Oslo Temp: -3` with one `fmt.Println` of four arguments.
3. Print `Welcome to Oslo!` with a string built from `city` using `+`.

Expected output:

```text
City: Oslo Temp: -3
Welcome to Oslo!
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	city := "Oslo"
	temp := -3
	fmt.Println("City:", city, "Temp:", temp)
	fmt.Println("Welcome to " + city + "!")
}

tests.output:
City: Oslo Temp: -3
Welcome to Oslo!

hints: `Println` adds the spaces for you: `fmt.Println("City:", city, ...)`.
`temp` is an int, so it cannot go in a `+` chain. It only belongs in the first line.

steps.title: Printf verbs
steps.body:
`fmt.Printf` takes a format string and fills each `%` verb with the next value, in order. It never adds a newline, so end every format with `\n`.

```go
fmt.Printf("%s is %d\n", "Ana", 9) // Ana is 9
```

| Verb | Prints |
| --- | --- |
| `%s` | a string |
| `%q` | a string in double quotes |
| `%d` | an integer |
| `%f` | a float, 6 decimals (`4.500000`) |
| `%.2f` | a float, 2 decimals (`4.50`) |
| `%t` | a bool |
| `%v` | any value in its default format |
| `%T` | the type of a value |
| `%%` | a literal `%` sign |

`%.2f` rounds to 2 decimals, which suits money. Avoid values exactly halfway, because Go rounds those to even: `%.1f` of 8.25 prints 8.2. A lone `%` starts a verb, so write `%%` for a percent sign.

A wrong verb or a missing value is not a compile error. The program compiles, runs anyway, and prints a marker in place of the value, such as `%!d(string=Tea)` for a string given to `%d`, or `%!s(MISSING)` when you run out of values. If you see `%!`, check that verbs and values line up.

example.title: Receipt line by line
example.prompt: Print each value of an order with the verb that fits it, then show what a wrong verb prints.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	item := "Tea"
	qty := 3
	price := 4.5
	paid := true
	fmt.Printf("Item: %s\n", item)
	fmt.Printf("Quoted: %q\n", item)
	fmt.Printf("Qty: %d\n", qty)
	fmt.Printf("Price: %.2f\n", price)
	fmt.Printf("Paid: %t\n", paid)
	fmt.Printf("All: %v %v %v\n", qty, price, paid)
	fmt.Printf("Discount: %d%%\n", 10)
	fmt.Printf("Type: %T\n", price)
	fmt.Printf("Oops: %d\n", item) // wrong verb for a string
}
example.output:
Item: Tea
Quoted: "Tea"
Qty: 3
Price: 4.50
Paid: true
All: 3 4.5 true
Discount: 10%
Type: float64
Oops: %!d(string=Tea)
example.explanation: Each `Printf` swaps its verbs for the values after the format, left to right. `%.2f` prints 4.5 with two decimals while `%v` prints it as plain `4.5`. In `%d%%` the `%d` takes 10 and `%%` prints one percent sign without using a value. `%T` reports `float64`, the default type for 4.5. The last line hands a string to `%d`, so Go prints a `%!d(...)` marker in its place. The program still compiles and runs.

practice.title: Movie log
practice.prompt:
Print a movie's details with Printf, one verb per line.

1. Print `Title: Dune` with `%s`, then `Quoted: "Dune"` with `%q`.
2. Print `Year: 2021` with `%d` and `Rating: 8.7` with `%.1f`.
3. Print `Watched: true` with `%t`, then `All: 2021 8.7 true` with three `%v`.
4. Print `Score: 95%` with `%d` and `%%`, then `Type: int` with `%T` of `year`.
5. End every format string with `\n`.

Expected output:

```text
Title: Dune
Quoted: "Dune"
Year: 2021
Rating: 8.7
Watched: true
All: 2021 8.7 true
Score: 95%
Type: int
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	title := "Dune"
	year := 2021
	rating := 8.7
	watched := true
	fmt.Printf("Title: %s\n", title)
	fmt.Printf("Quoted: %q\n", title)
	fmt.Printf("Year: %d\n", year)
	fmt.Printf("Rating: %.1f\n", rating)
	fmt.Printf("Watched: %t\n", watched)
	fmt.Printf("All: %v %v %v\n", year, rating, watched)
	fmt.Printf("Score: %d%%\n", 95)
	fmt.Printf("Type: %T\n", year)
}

tests.output:
Title: Dune
Quoted: "Dune"
Year: 2021
Rating: 8.7
Watched: true
All: 2021 8.7 true
Score: 95%
Type: int

hints: Copy the shape of the example: one `fmt.Printf("Label: %verb\n", value)` per line.
A lone `%` would start a verb. Write `%%` to print one percent sign.
If you see `%!` in your output, a verb and its value do not match.

steps.title: Widths and Sprintf
steps.body:
A number between `%` and the verb sets a minimum width. Values shorter than the width get padded with spaces, which lines up columns.

```go
fmt.Printf("[%5d]\n", 42)    // [   42] right-aligned
fmt.Printf("[%-6s]\n", "Go") // [Go    ] left-aligned
fmt.Printf("[%05d]\n", 42)   // [00042] zero-padded
fmt.Printf("[%8.2f]\n", 3.5) // [    3.50]
```

Every value right-aligns by default, strings included, and a `-` flips that to the left, which suits names. A leading `0` pads with zeros instead of spaces. With floats, `%8.2f` combines width and precision: 8 columns in total counting the point, 2 of them decimals. Width is a minimum, so a longer value is never cut. It just pushes the columns out.

`fmt.Sprintf` takes the same format and values but returns the string instead of printing it. Use it to build text you want to store, join with `+`, or print later.

```go
label := fmt.Sprintf("ID-%03d", 7) // "ID-007"
```

example.title: Price table
example.prompt: Print a header and three aligned price rows, then build an order number with Sprintf.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Printf("%-8s%7s\n", "Item", "Price")
	fmt.Printf("%-8s%7.2f\n", "Tea", 4.5)
	fmt.Printf("%-8s%7.2f\n", "Coffee", 12.25)
	fmt.Printf("%-8s%7.2f\n", "Cake", 105.0)
	order := fmt.Sprintf("Order #%05d", 42)
	fmt.Println(order)
}
example.output:
Item      Price
Tea        4.50
Coffee    12.25
Cake     105.00
Order #00042
example.explanation: `%-8s` pads every name on the right to 8 columns, so each price starts in the same place. `%7.2f` right-aligns the price in 7 columns with 2 decimals, so the decimal points line up, and the header uses `%7s` to match. `105.0` is written as a float because `%f` needs one. `Sprintf` returns `Order #00042` as a string, padded to 5 digits by `%05d`, and `Println` prints it.

practice.title: Scoreboard
practice.prompt:
Print an aligned scoreboard with points and accuracy, then build a player tag with Sprintf.

1. Keep the header line from the starter.
2. Print rows for `Ana` 120 87.5, `Bruno` 95 64.0, and `Chen` 7 92.3, with names in `%-10s`, points in `%5d`, and accuracy in `%8.1f`.
3. Build the string `Player 007` from the number 7 with `fmt.Sprintf` and `%03d`, store it in a variable, and print it with `fmt.Println`.

Expected output:

```text
Player      Pts     Acc
Ana         120    87.5
Bruno        95    64.0
Chen          7    92.3
Player 007
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Printf("%-10s%5s%8s\n", "Player", "Pts", "Acc")
	fmt.Printf("%-10s%5d%8.1f\n", "Ana", 120, 87.5)
	fmt.Printf("%-10s%5d%8.1f\n", "Bruno", 95, 64.0)
	fmt.Printf("%-10s%5d%8.1f\n", "Chen", 7, 92.3)
	player := fmt.Sprintf("Player %03d", 7)
	fmt.Println(player)
}

tests.output:
Player      Pts     Acc
Ana         120    87.5
Bruno        95    64.0
Chen          7    92.3
Player 007

hints: Reuse the header's format for each row, but swap `%5s` for `%5d` because the points are ints, and `%8s` for `%8.1f` because the accuracy is a float.
Write Bruno's accuracy as `64.0`, not `64`, because `%f` needs a float.
`Sprintf` returns a string, so assign it with `:=` and pass that variable to `Println`.

recap:
- `fmt.Println("Label:", value)` puts a space between arguments and ends the line.
- `+` joins strings only. `"Age: " + 30` does not compile.
- `Printf` verbs: `%s` `%q` `%d` `%f` `%.2f` `%t` `%v` `%T`, and `%%` for a percent sign.
- `Printf` never adds a newline, so end formats with `\n`.
- A mismatched or missing value prints a `%!` marker instead of failing to compile.
- `%5d` right-aligns, `%-10s` left-aligns, `%05d` zero-pads, `%8.2f` sets width and precision.
- `fmt.Sprintf` returns the formatted string instead of printing it.
